name: Diverging Directions
description: You are given a directed weighted graph with n nodes and 2 n - 2 edges. The nodes are labeled from 1 to n , while the edges are labeled from 1 to 2 n - 2 . The graph's edges can be split into two parts. The first n - 1 edges will form a rooted spanning tree, with node 1 as the root. All these edges will point away from the root. The last n - 1 edges will be from node i to node 1 , for all 2 ≤ i ≤ n . You are given q queries. There are two types of queries 1 i w : Change the weight of the i -th edge to w 2 u v : Print the length of the shortest path between nodes u to v Given these queries, print the shortest path lengths.
input_specification: The first line of input will contain two integers n , q ( 2 ≤ n , q ≤ 200 000 ), the number of nodes, and the number of queries, respectively. The next 2 n - 2 integers will contain 3 integers a i , b i , c i , denoting a directed edge from node a i to node b i with weight c i . The first n - 1 of these lines will describe a rooted spanning tree pointing away from node 1 , while the last n - 1 of these lines will have b i = 1 . More specifically, The edges ( a 1 , b 1 ), ( a 2 , b 2 ), ... ( a n - 1 , b n - 1 ) will describe a rooted spanning tree pointing away from node 1 . b j = 1 for n ≤ j ≤ 2 n - 2 . a n , a n + 1 , ..., a 2 n - 2 will be distinct and between 2 and n . The next q lines will contain 3 integers, describing a query in the format described in the statement. All edge weights will be between 1 and 10 6 .
output_specification: For each type 2 query, print the length of the shortest path in its own line.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 838B — Diverging Directions [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
